description: People who are interested in STEM, space, and building cool stuff. We’re here to tackle a NASA challenge, learn some new things, and see what we can come up with.
summary:
Mars Bound is a 2D, pixel-art survival game where players take on the challenge of keeping an abandoned Mars base running. Stranded in Gale Crater after their crew leaves without them, players must survive for 10 sols until the next crew arrives.

To survive, players manage essential resources like oxygen, power, food, water, heat and health while keeping eight base stations operational. Each station comes with its own challenges, including timed repairs and interactive minigames, such as aiming UHF signals at an orbiting spacecraft. Players must also choose between solar, nuclear or hybrid power systems, each with its own advantages and trade-offs.

The game features an explorable map inspired by Curiosity's real landing site in Gale Crater, with ten unique zones to discover. Along the way, players unlock facts about real Mars missions, from Curiosity's 2012 landing to MOXIE's success in producing oxygen on Perseverance. With a seven-page How to Play guide, hints and a high-score system, Mars Bound makes learning accessible and fun.

Our goal is to help kids understand what it really takes to survive on Mars through hands-on gameplay, while showing how the technologies needed for space exploration can also benefit life on Earth.
details:
What it does / how it works

Mars Bound is a 2D, top-down pixel-art survival game where players take on the role of a junior astronaut stranded in Gale Crater after their crew's ascent vehicle leaves without them. Their mission is to keep an abandoned Mars base running for 10 sols (Martian days) until the next crew arrives.

Players must keep five essential survival systems running: air, power, food, heat and health. These systems are connected, so if one starts failing, it can affect the others. For example, losing power can affect oxygen production and heating, eventually putting the astronaut's health at risk.

The game has eight stations to maintain: Solar, Reactor, MOXIE, Water, Radio, Battery, Habitat and Garden. Players explore the base, complete timed repair jobs and play minigames to keep everything working. These include aiming a radio dish at an orbiting spacecraft and fixing damaged equipment by keeping a moving line in the correct zone.

Players can also explore the map, collect materials such as iron, sand, clay and water ice, and use them to build additional solar panels, MOXIE units, gardens and battery banks. At the beginning, they must choose between solar, reactor or hybrid power, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.

The game takes place in one continuous, explorable map inspired by Curiosity's real landing site in Gale Crater. It includes ten locations, such as Bradbury Landing, Rocknest and Mount Sharp. The map is stylised rather than geographically accurate in scale. As players explore, they unlock discovery cards explaining the real science and history behind different locations, materials and technologies.

To make the game accessible to younger players, we included a seven-page How to Play guide, hints, on-screen instructions and a goals panel. Players receive a final score based on their performance, giving them a reason to improve and try different strategies in future runs.

Benefits

  • Learning through experience: Instead of simply reading about how a Mars base works, kids get to experience the challenges themselves. They can see what happens when power runs low, oxygen production stops or the habitat loses heat.
  • Understanding connected systems: Players learn that a Mars settlement depends on many systems working together. For example, keeping the garden running requires power, but that same power is needed for heating and life support.
  • Encouraging problem-solving: Timed repairs, unexpected events and limited resources encourage players to make decisions and think ahead.
  • Designed for younger audiences: The simple controls, colourful pixel-art world, hints and short challenges make the game approachable for kids aged 5–12.
  • Making science interesting: Discovery cards introduce players to real NASA missions and technologies, including Curiosity, Perseverance, MOXIE, Phoenix and the ISS Veggie experiment.

Intended impact

Our goal is to get younger students interested in space exploration, science and engineering by giving them a chance to experience what it takes to operate a settlement on Mars.

We also wanted to show that the challenges astronauts face in space are connected to problems we face on Earth. Technologies such as more reliable batteries, dust-resistant solar panels, water recycling and efficient food production could also help communities here at home.

Ultimately, we want to make the connection between what students learn in the classroom and how those ideas are used to solve real-world problems. We hope Mars Bound encourages kids to think beyond simply surviving on Mars and start imagining how they could help make future space exploration possible.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software used

  • Platform: A web-based game hosted on Vercel, accessible through a regular desktop or laptop browser without downloading anything. Play Mars Bound
  • Hardware: A standard computer and keyboard. No additional equipment is required.
  • Game design: A 2D, top-down pixel-art style inspired by Google's Champion Island and Overcooked. Players explore, collect resources and complete tasks under time limits.
  • Research: We used resources including NASA Mars Trek, NASA Open APIs, DONKI, the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), RadLab and Canadian Space Agency STEM resources.
  • Team collaboration: We used a shared Google Doc to organize research, divide responsibilities and develop the game's framework. Team members researched different areas, including power, temperature, life support, resource utilization (ISRU), communication delays and survival challenges.
  • AI assistance: AI tools were used to assist with coding and development.

How is it creative?

We wanted to do more than create another science quiz or simulation. Instead of just telling players how a Mars settlement works, we put them in the astronaut's position and let them experience the challenges firsthand.

One of our main design choices was combining an open-world exploration game with time-sensitive tasks. Players can freely explore Gale Crater, but they also have to keep track of their resources and respond to emergencies before time runs out.

We also made scientific discoveries part of the gameplay. Rather than presenting all the information at once, players unlock facts about real Mars missions and technologies as they explore. Combined with different power strategies, repair minigames and a high-score system, this makes learning more interactive and encourages players to try different approaches each time they play.

What factors did your team consider?

While developing Mars Bound, we considered several challenges that astronauts would face when living and working on Mars:

  • Power: Mars receives less sunlight than Earth, and dust storms can reduce solar energy production. We considered the advantages and disadvantages of solar, nuclear and hybrid power systems, as well as the importance of energy storage.
  • Temperature: Temperatures on Mars can change dramatically between day and night. We considered how astronauts would keep their habitats warm while managing limited power.
  • Life support: Astronauts need a reliable supply of oxygen, clean water and food. We researched technologies such as MOXIE, which demonstrated how oxygen could be produced from the carbon dioxide in Mars' atmosphere.
  • Radiation and dust: Mars has a thin atmosphere and limited protection from radiation. Dust can also interfere with equipment, especially solar panels. We considered shielding, dust removal and emergency shelter systems.
  • Communication delays: Messages between Earth and Mars can take approximately 3–22 minutes one way. This means astronauts cannot always wait for instructions from Mission Control and must be able to make decisions independently.
  • In-situ resource utilization (ISRU): We explored how astronauts could use materials already available on Mars, such as water ice and regolith, rather than relying entirely on supplies from Earth.
  • Crew health and safety: Food, water, oxygen, temperature, exercise and backup systems all play a role in keeping astronauts healthy and safe.
  • Kid-friendly design: Since our target audience is ages 5–12, we focused on simple controls, understandable instructions and interactive challenges that introduce scientific concepts without overwhelming younger players.
